did_you_know.text: Did you know? The events in this chapter take place in the tenth year of Zedekiah’s reign, which was the eighteenth year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon.
Did you know? Jeremiah was commanded to buy the field at Anathoth because he had the right of redemption—the family right to purchase the land.
Did you know? Jeremiah paid Hanamel seven shekels and ten pieces of silver for the field, and then weighed out the silver on scales.
Did you know? After the transaction was completed, Baruch son of Neriah was commanded to store the deed of purchase in a clay jar so that it would last a long time.
Did you know? In his prayer, Jeremiah recalls that the LORD created the heavens and the earth, and therefore nothing is too difficult or impossible for him.
Did you know? In this chapter, the LORD identifies himself as the “God of all mankind” and asks, “Is anything too difficult for me?”—a question emphasizing his ability to fulfill his promises.

Did you know? Alongside the promise of destruction, the LORD promises to gather his people from all the countries to which he had banished them and bring them back to this place so that they may live in safety.

Did you know? The chapter ends by describing a future in which fields will once again be bought with money, deeds will be written and sealed, and witnesses will be called in the land of Benjamin, in Jerusalem, and in the towns of Judah—because the LORD will restore the fortunes of his people.
